Imagine a parfait glass with neat, distinct bands of yogurt at the bottom, granola in the middle, and fruit on top — each ingredient sitting in its own separate layer, none of them blended together. That arrangement of distinct, ordered layers is the heart of what "stratification" means.

Stratification is the arrangement of something into distinct, separate layers or levels — stacked in an ordered way, one above the other. It can describe the process of those layers forming, or the resulting condition of being layered.
What makes it "stratification" and not just "layering"?

The layers in stratification have specific qualities:

  • They are distinct — clearly separated, not blurred into each other
  • They are ordered — arranged in a sequence from bottom to top (or top to bottom)
  • They are stable — they persist over time, they don't just collapse or dissolve
  • They are often hierarchical — especially in human and social contexts, some layers rank "above" or "below" others in terms of power, value, or privilege

1. In geology and earth science (the most literal use)

Look at a cliff face and you'll often see distinct horizontal bands of rock in different colors and textures. Each band is a layer — called a stratum (singular) or strata (plural). These layers formed over millions of years as sediments (sand, mud, minerals) settled and hardened, with each era leaving its own mark. The resulting stacked structure is geological stratification.

Geologists read these layers like pages in a history book: older layers sit deeper down, newer ones lie on top. The order tells them when things happened and what conditions existed at each time.

2. In society — social stratification (the most common everyday use)

This is where you'll hear the word most. Social stratification is the way a society divides into distinct groups or classes based on wealth, power, status, or education — like a layered cake where each layer represents a different tier of society.

The upper layers hold more resources and privilege; the lower layers hold less. What makes this "stratification" rather than just "difference" is that:

  • The layers are systematic and persistent — they don't form randomly or briefly
  • They are often inherited — you're usually born into a layer, and it's hard to move out of it
  • They carry real consequences — your layer affects your healthcare, education, life expectancy, and opportunities

Classic examples: feudal systems (nobility on top, serfs at the bottom), caste systems (where your birth caste locked you into a layer for life), and modern economic class systems (upper class, middle class, working class, underclass).

Social mobility — the ability to move from one layer to another — is the opposite of rigid stratification. A society with high stratification and low mobility means most people stay in the layer they were born into. A society with low stratification means the layers are more fluid and crossable.

3. In the atmosphere

Earth's atmosphere is divided into distinct layers — the troposphere (where we breathe and weather happens), the stratosphere (where jets fly and the ozone layer sits), the mesosphere, the thermosphere, and the exosphere. Each layer has different temperature, pressure, and chemical characteristics.

This ordered, layered structure of the atmosphere is called atmospheric stratification.

4. In lakes and bodies of water

A deep lake can become thermally stratified: warm, lighter water floats on top, and cold, dense water settles at the bottom. These layers don't mix easily. This matters because oxygen and nutrients distribute unevenly across the layers, affecting fish and plant life throughout the water. When seasons change and the layers break down and mix, it's called a "turnover."

5. In forests and ecosystems

A forest is naturally stratified into vertical layers: the canopy (tall trees reaching for sunlight at the top), the understory (shorter trees beneath), the shrub layer, the herb and grass layer, and the forest floor. Each layer receives different amounts of light, moisture, and temperature — and supports different species of plants and animals. This is vegetation stratification.

6. In statistics and research

Researchers studying a large population (say, all adults in India) often divide that population into meaningful sub-groups — by age, income, region, or gender — before selecting their study sample. This act of intentionally dividing a population into distinct sub-groups is called stratification. It ensures every important group is fairly represented in the data, making results more accurate. The technique is called stratified sampling.

7. In medicine

Doctors use risk stratification — sorting patients into groups (low-risk, medium-risk, high-risk) based on how likely they are to develop a disease or complication. This helps allocate treatment and monitoring appropriately. The "layers" here are conceptual rather than physical, but the logic is the same: distinct, ordered groups arranged by level.
Process vs. state — both are valid

The word can work two ways:

  • As a process: "The stratification of rock occurred over millions of years." (describing the act of layers forming over time)
  • As a state/condition: "The stratification of that society is very rigid." (describing the current condition of being divided into layers)

Both are correct. Context makes the meaning clear.

In physical science (rock, atmosphere, forest), layers are simply different — the top layer isn't necessarily "better" than the bottom one. But in social and human contexts, stratification almost always carries a rank. The top layers enjoy more power, wealth, and opportunity than the bottom layers. This is why social stratification is closely linked to inequality.

Stratification = the arrangement (or resulting condition) of something into distinct, ordered, stable layers or levels.

  • Physically: rock bands, atmospheric zones, forest canopies, water temperature layers
  • Socially: classes, castes, economic tiers — with hierarchy and inequality baked in
  • Analytically: dividing a population or group of patients into sub-groups for study or treatment

Whenever you see the word, the central image to hold onto is always the same: things divided into neat, ordered, separate layers — each layer different from the one above and below it, and all of them stacked in a recognizable sequence.
